But philosophy could still possess only partial, though genuinely true, knowledge of the real and material world of things.
If philosophy must necessarily aim at omniscience or “wisdom,” this is ultimately because its primary concern is not things, but the human being.

As we have already said—though we have not yet proved it—human beings differ from things, whether real or ideal, because they have no fixed and unchanging qualities given once and for all. Human beings are essentially historical: they change in fundamental ways over time.

If that is so, then there is simply no such thing as the general concept of “the human being,” or “humanity in general.” “Iron in general” has always been and always will be what it is. So if we know what iron is, we already know something about any particular piece of iron, even one that does not yet exist.

But there is no equivalent “human being in general” whose nature would tell us, even partly, what a person in the Stone Age was like, or an Athenian in the age of Pericles, or a medieval Christian, or a person in contemporary Russia—still less a person living in the year 5000.

Imagine that over the centuries iron had changed its density, atomic number, and valence. In that case there would hardly be any “iron in general” at all, and knowledge of such a thing would be impossible. Grouping all these different “irons” under a single general concept would make about as much sense as trying to find one common concept for a cow, the Moon, and a staircase.

Historical changes in human beings are so great and so fundamental that knowing whatever eternal qualities human beings might have would tell us nothing about actual human beings. Nor can there be perfectly or absolutely true partial knowledge of them. Even if we knew everything human beings had been up to the present, we still could not say that these were their eternal qualities, or that knowing them amounted to genuine, if partial, knowledge.
Human beings can still change radically. They can change so much that something which had always been true of them ceases to be true.

This means that humanity can be known only concretely: by knowing real humanity as it actually exists through its history. There can be no abstract knowledge of “humanity in general.” And since philosophy seeks to know humanity, it must seek concrete knowledge. Since every genuinely concrete knowledge is knowledge of a whole, philosophy must therefore aim at omniscience, or “wisdom.”

All philosophy before Hegel failed to see clearly that human existence is historical and “non-thing-like.” Because of this, it could not explain why philosophy necessarily aims at omniscience. Philosophers sought “wisdom,” but they did so instinctively and, so to speak, without fully understanding why. They therefore had no satisfactory answer to the question of why they were seeking it. As a result, they also had only a very imperfect idea of the means or method required to reach omniscience, and they did not clearly understand what omniscience itself would have to be like.

At first, philosophers simply hoped to exhaust everything that could be known by listing it all without any particular order. It soon became obvious that omniscience could not be reached in this way. So attempts were made to organize, or “systematize,” philosophical inquiry.

Knowledge was divided into fields and subfields. This made it possible, first, to identify the subjects that had to be studied and the order in which to study them and, second, to give some definite structure to the future totality of knowledge.
This is how the idea of a philosophical “system” arose.

“Wisdom,” or omniscience—that is, perfect knowledge—is not a disordered collection of separate pieces of knowledge. It is an organized whole with definite parts. These parts occupy a definite place within the whole, and they depend on one another in definite ways.

Once philosophy began to aim at “wisdom,” it therefore began to aim at a complete system of knowledge, while trying, as far as possible, to give philosophy itself the same systematic form that wisdom would have.
The origins of “systematic philosophy” disappear, as the saying goes, into the mists of time. But it was only in the Roman period that philosophy began to take a more or less systematic form.

The Stoics, for example, introduced what later became the classical division of philosophy into logic, physics, and ethics: doctrines concerning knowledge, the real natural world, and the real human world.
We also find attempts to construct philosophical “systems” among the Neoplatonists, the Gnostics, the medieval Scholastics, and all the major “modern” philosophers.
Finally, Hegel produced the most fully self-conscious system of all.

Every philosopher before Hegel assumed that everything that exists exists in the manner of a thing, whether real or ideal. But human beings, as Hegel clearly understood, exist in a fundamentally different way: as historical beings.
It follows that Hegel’s idea of a “complete system of knowledge,” or of wisdom, differs fundamentally from every earlier one.
We must therefore distinguish not one but two types of philosophical system, both of which have been offered as omniscience or wisdom.

Spinoza’s Ethics is the most fully developed pre-Hegelian system. We should therefore look at it now as the model for all systems that claimed to provide omniscience while assuming that everything we can know exists like a thing with eternal and unchanging qualities.
The most characteristic feature of systems of the Spinozist type is that they exclude time completely, and with time they exclude all development and movement.
The reason is easy to understand.

If everything that exists exists like a thing, and if each thing can be defined once and for all by unchanging qualities, then complete knowledge of everything that exists simply means complete knowledge of these eternal qualities.
Time therefore has no place in the system.
And because all these qualities exist simultaneously, movement and development have no place in it either.
This is why Spinoza took geometry as his model for a philosophical system. Geometry also contains neither time nor movement. Its definitions, axioms, and theorems all exist together, timelessly.
Of course, in a geometrical presentation, theorems come one after another and are “derived” from one another. But this is, so to speak, only because of human “imperfection.”

If we knew all the definitions and axioms completely, then in a sense we would already know all the theorems immediately. They are all contained in the axioms, so deriving them adds nothing fundamentally new.
We therefore possess a complete or perfect geometrical system as soon as we possess the complete list of its definitions and axioms.
From these we can, if we wish, derive every possible theorem and so learn everything that can be known about the geometrical world.

And because this whole world exists all at once—or, more precisely, outside time, “eternally”—all possible knowledge of it is already contained completely and immediately in the total set of geometrical definitions and axioms.
The definitions establish, so to speak, the “boundaries” of the geometrical world, while the axioms establish its “laws.”
If we know the definitions, we know what kinds of “things” can belong to the geometrical world and what kinds cannot.

So if we know the nature of all the “things” that can make up the world of geometry, and if we also know all the laws governing their possible combinations, then we know everything about that world that can possibly be known.
Spinoza’s philosophical system differs from a geometrical system only in one respect: in principle, it includes all knowledge, not merely knowledge of one particular domain of being.

The list of philosophical definitions must therefore exhaust the fundamental qualities of all things, both real and ideal, that exist at all. And the list of philosophical axioms must contain all the fundamental laws governing the possible interactions between things.

But if the list of definitions and axioms is genuinely complete, then all knowledge can in principle be “derived” from it with relatively little further work. We would then be able to give a satisfactory answer to any meaningful question that could possibly be asked.

It has to be said that Spinoza, like most philosophers before Hegel, overlooked the difficulties that appear as soon as we are talking about omniscience rather than knowledge of some particular part of everything that exists.
Geometry, for example, studies precisely those “things”—and only those things—that fall under its definitions and are governed by its axioms.
The geometer knows perfectly well that other, non-geometrical things exist, but is simply not interested in them.

This is why producing a “complete” list of geometrical definitions and axioms is not especially difficult. The definitions and axioms need only satisfy two conditions: they must not contradict one another, and they must define at least one possible group of existing ideal “things.” The geometer can then study those things and those things alone.
But the philosopher who wants to know everything is in a very different position.
The geometer more or less determines the object of study by choosing a set of definitions and axioms.
The philosopher, by contrast, has to fit the definitions and axioms to an object that has already been given.

And since that “object” is everything that exists, the scale of the task becomes obvious. The philosopher’s list of definitions and axioms would have to be complete and exhaustive in every possible sense.

Philosophers who tried to construct systems of the Spinozist type never explained what method should be used to discover the philosophical definitions and axioms. Nor did they explain how one could establish that these definitions and axioms did not contradict one another, or even how one could know that the list was really complete.
They simply assumed, without saying so, that such a list could be found by enumeration.

They did understand that it was impossible to enumerate every individual thing in existence, as the earliest philosophers had hoped to do. But they believed that the qualities shared identically by all things were very few in number and could therefore be listed completely.
This was supposed to give us the complete list of philosophical definitions.
All the diversity of particular things would then result from different combinations of these fundamental qualities, in accordance with certain eternal laws.
These fundamental laws were also assumed to be few in number, and each was thought to be immediately “self-evident.”
So philosophers assumed that they could find within our own “reason” all the “self-evident truths” required to make up the complete list of philosophical axioms.
After that, there would in principle be no insurmountable difficulty.
But as we will soon see, a Spinozist system of this kind is impossible not only in practice but in principle.
On the one hand, there is simply no rigorous way of proving that a supposedly complete list of definitions and axioms really is exhaustive.
On the other hand—and this is much more serious—such a list is impossible in principle for the simple reason that there are no “self-evident truths,” and therefore no axioms of this kind at all.
Anyone who is free from prejudice knows perfectly well that they can be mistaken even when they are completely “certain” that what they are saying is true and even when it seems “self-evident.”
They also know that something which seems “self-evident” to one person may not seem self-evident to another.
The idea that a person can examine their own “reason” and, before observing the real world, discover self-evident truths about that world—supposedly a priori truths—is simply false.
Unless a proposition is tested against experience, there is no way to determine whether it is true.
So the very idea of the Spinozist system is plainly unsound because it rests on a false assumption.
There is another way to show why it is impossible in principle.

When we are dealing with the world of existing things, whether real or ideal, a complete system of axioms is at least conceivable. We may not be able to establish such a system independently of experience, since we can never be sure that the system we have found is genuinely complete. But it is at least possible to imagine one.
With the human or historical world, however, no such system is even conceivable.
The reason is simple: there are no mathematical-style definitions or axioms that apply to human beings.

Because human beings are historical, because their qualities change, there can be no definitions fixed once and for all that establish the properties of a human being. Nor can there be eternal laws or axioms that forever determine how human beings interact with the natural world and with one another.
A philosophical system must be complete. But human beings cannot possibly be fitted into a Spinozist system modeled on geometry.
A completely different, non-mathematical kind of system is therefore required.
Hegel discovered this specifically philosophical kind of system.

We will not examine Hegel’s system in detail here. First, because there will be plenty of opportunity to do so later. Second, because this entire book is itself an example of Hegelian system-building.
But a few things should be said now.
Systems of the Spinozist type take things, whether real or ideal, as their model and are therefore characterized by the absence of time and movement.
Hegel’s system, by contrast, takes human beings as its model and is characterized precisely by the presence of time and movement.

Because human beings are essentially historical, philosophical omniscience must include knowledge of humanity. It must therefore include the history of humanity and, with it, the time in which that history unfolds.

And because human beings have no unchanging qualities given once and for all, but instead exist through constant development and temporal change, a philosophical system must itself have the character of a developing and moving whole.
Omniscience is therefore not complete at the beginning, as it is in Spinoza, in a collection of definitions and axioms presented from the outset.
It coincides instead with the system as a whole and develops gradually as the system itself develops.
Omniscience is not found at the beginning but at the end. It is not the source of the system’s development but its result.

Hegel called this distinctive feature of his system dialectic: its concepts are not given once and for all at the beginning, but gradually develop and emerge from one another, as though reproducing the historical and temporal development of what exists.

Hegel’s system is “realist,” not “idealist,” in the sense that it does not take its concepts from a supposedly self-contained human “reason” independent of the real world, whether natural or historical.
It takes them from the world itself—a world that exists independently of reason and is “revealed” to knowledge only in or through reason.

On the one hand, Hegel’s system necessarily includes knowledge of human history. On the other hand, its logical structure reflects the temporal process of real development and movement within reality itself.
Hegelian realism can therefore be called “historical” or “dialectical”—as Marx, his great disciple, later called his own realism.
Because Hegel’s system is historical and dialectical, it has two important features that we should note here.
First, Hegel does away with the false philosophical idea of “axioms,” or truths that are supposedly self-evident and independent of experience.
No individual proposition within the system is in itself “self-evident.” Some of them can even seem completely implausible when taken on their own.
